angleRead.name: Elliot Marbury
angleRead.text: I keep coming back to the strikeout rate. Nine seasons on the dossier, and the one number that moves is the whiff. In 2036, one every 5.3 AB. 2037, 5.2. 2038, 5.1. Then it loosens — 7.9 in the short 2039, 6.7 in 2040, 6.6 in 2041. The power stayed. The walks stayed. The batting average came back. But the strikeouts stopped coming at the old clip, and I want to know if that's a choice or a change. The 2039 season is the hinge — 90 games, 348 at-bats, one homer every 13.9 AB. That's the best power rate on the sheet, and it's also the smallest sample. A thin season is variance, not identity. plan.focus: Martin Richards' strikeout rate decline across 2039-2041 and what it means for his profile as the A's weigh everyday at-bats at third base.
plan.why: The strikeout rate is the only column that moved persistently across the dossier. Power, walks, and average all oscillate around established norms; the whiff rate stepped down and stayed down. That's the kind of shift that changes how a front office values a player, especially with a younger peer on the same position showing an extreme version of the same trait.
checks: Pull Richards' strikeout rate for each of the nine seasons on the dossier and confirm the step-down begins in 2039.
Verify the 2039 season is the smallest sample (90 G, 348 AB) and flag it as the weak link in the trend.
Compare Richards' 2040-41 strikeout rates against his 2036-38 rates to establish the size of the shift.
Note Kevin Clark's 2041 strikeout rate (1 per 21.3 AB) as the peer contrast, with his 64-AB sample size stated.
Check whether the walk rate and power rate stayed stable across the same period, to isolate strikeouts as the variable.
plan.interpretation: The numbers suggest a hitter who stopped chasing. The strikeout rate dropped by roughly a quarter from its peak years while the production stayed. That could be a conscious adjustment, a change in approach, or just the natural arc of a veteran who learned to spoil pitches. The 2039 season is the fulcrum — it's the best power rate and the worst sample. If you read the trend from 2036 forward, it looks like a correction. unverifiedLead: Whether Richards changed his approach at the plate starting in 2039 — possibly related to the reduced games that season — is not in the dossier and would need a conversation with someone who watched him daily.
Whether the organization's preference for contact is a factor in how Richards is evaluated this offseason is suggested by the Kevin Clark comparison but not confirmed by any team statement.
plan.closeQuestion: If Richards' strikeout rate stays around one per 6.5 AB next season, does he become a more valuable asset than the raw numbers suggest — and does that change how the A's should think about the position?
